walkthroughs.body_html:
Finance and Accounts — a core area of Business Studies.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Finance and Accounts brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Finance and Accounts.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Luca Pacioli's 'Summa de Arithmetica' detailing double-entry bookkeeping dates from:

options: Payback
Average rate of return
Net present value
Accounting rate

mcqs.q: Why can a profitable business run out of cash?
options: Break-even is when machines break down evenly.
Because profit counts credit sales and ignores timing — if customers pay slowly while wages, rent and suppliers demand cash now, the firm can become insolvent despite profits.
Cash shortages only happen to charities.
Profitable businesses always have enough cash.

mcqs.q: Is break-even the point where a business becomes successful?
options: Revenue is the money owed to the tax office.
Break-even is when machines break down evenly.
It is only where total revenue equals total costs — no profit, no loss; success depends on how far sales exceed it (the margin of safety) and on wider objectives.
Reaching break-even means the business is now profitable.

mcqs.q: Is revenue the same as profit?
options: Revenue is the money owed to the tax office.
Break-even is when machines break down evenly.
No — revenue is income from sales (price times quantity); profit is what remains after all costs are subtracted, so high revenue can coexist with losses.
A business with millions in sales must be making millions in profit.
